Lab 2: Regression in R

Intermediate Quantitative Methods · Week 2

Author

Sebastian Ramirez-Ruiz

Term

Autumn 2026

Welcome! 👋

In this week’s seminar we asked what a regression is for. Is it description, prediction, or causal inference? The same line of code, lm(y ~ x), means different things depending on the answer.

In this lab we get our hands dirty with regression in R. We will run one substantive example from start to finish:

How are education and attitudes toward immigration related in Europe?

This is a classic question in both political science and sociology (e.g., Hainmueller & Hiscox 2007), and it is a good one for learning. The association is strong, the mechanisms are contested, and a causal interpretation is tempting and hard to defend.

Plan for today ≈ time
Setup and data preparation 10 min
Bivariate regression: syntax, output, interpretation 25 min
Binary and categorical predictors 15 min
Multiple regression and “holding constant” (regression anatomy) 20 min
Interactions and predictions with {marginaleffects} 15 min
Uncertainty: robust, clustered, and bootstrapped standard errors 15 min
Regression tables with {modelsummary} 10 min

Packages 📦

# Install these in your CONSOLE if you have not done so yet:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven", "broom", "modelsummary", "marginaleffects"))

library(tidyverse) # data wrangling and visualization
library(haven) # to read the ESS Stata file
library(broom) # to turn model output into tidy data frames
library(modelsummary) # to create regression tables
library(marginaleffects) # to compute predictions, slopes, and comparisons

Data preparation 🧹

We use the same ESS Round 11 subset as last week. Our outcome is:

  • imwbcnt: “Is [country] made a worse or a better place to live by people coming to live here from other countries?” (0 = worse place, 10 = better place).

Our main explanatory variable is years of full-time education (eduyrs).

The cleaning pipeline below applies last week’s {dplyr} skills. Read it line by line. Every line is a research decision.

ess <- haven::read_dta("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seramirezruiz/seramirezruiz.github.io/master/data/ess11_lab.dta") %>%
  haven::zap_labels() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    eduyrs = dplyr::if_else(eduyrs > 25, 25, eduyrs), # top-code implausible values
    female = dplyr::if_else(gndr == 2, 1, 0),
    born_abroad = dplyr::if_else(brncntr == 2, 1, 0),
    residence = dplyr::case_when(
      domicil %in% 1:2 ~ "Big city",
      domicil == 3 ~ "Town",
      domicil %in% 4:5 ~ "Rural"
    ),
    residence = factor(residence, levels = c("Big city", "Town", "Rural"))
  )

A common analysis sample

lm() silently drops every row with a missing value in any variable in the model (listwise deletion). If we compare models with different variables, they will be estimated on different samples, and differences in coefficients may come from the sample, not the specification.

The fix is to define the analysis sample once:

ess_reg <- ess %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(imwbcnt, eduyrs, agea, female, born_abroad, hinctnta, residence)

nrow(ess)
[1] 40156
nrow(ess_reg)
[1] 30611

Activity 💡

We lost almost a quarter of the sample. Which variable is responsible for most of it? Why might that be a problem for what we can say about the population?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess %>%
  dplyr::summarize(dplyr::across(c(imwbcnt, eduyrs, agea, hinctnta, residence),
                                 \(x) sum(is.na(x))))

Household income (hinctnta) accounts for most of the missingness. Income non-response is rarely random: it is typically higher among the very rich, the very poor, and in some countries more than others. Our complete-case sample is not a random subsample of the ESS. This is a first taste of how measurement and missing data (Weeks 4–5) shape what our regressions can tell us.

Bivariate regression 📈

Look before you regress 👀

A linear regression is an approximation to the conditional expectation function (CEF): the average of \(Y\) at each value of \(X\). Let’s look at the CEF directly by computing the mean attitude at each year of education, then drawing the OLS line on top:

cef <- ess_reg %>%
  dplyr::group_by(eduyrs) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_imm = mean(imwbcnt), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cef, aes(x = eduyrs, y = mean_imm)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#2f1a61", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(data = ess_reg, aes(x = eduyrs, y = imwbcnt),
              method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#cc0065") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Years of full-time education",
       y = "Immigrants make country a better place (0-10)",
       size = "Respondents",
       title = "Mean attitude by years of education, with the OLS line")

The line summarizes the conditional means well in the middle, where most of the data are. The extremes, with very few respondents, are noisy.

The lm() function

The relationship we want to estimate is:

\[Immigration\ attitude_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Education_i + \epsilon_i\]

The general syntax for running a regression model in R is:

your_model_biv <- lm(outcome ~ explanatory_variable, data = your_data)
your_model_mult <- lm(outcome ~ explanatory_1 + explanatory_2, data = your_data)

The ~ (tilde) separates the outcome from the predictors. This is R’s formula syntax, which you will see in almost every modeling function: glm(), lme4::lmer(), fixest::feols(), and so on.

model_1 <- lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs, data = ess_reg)
model_1

Call:
lm(formula = imwbcnt ~ eduyrs, data = ess_reg)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)       eduyrs  
      3.262        0.146

Printing the model only shows the coefficients. model_1 is a list that contains much more (residuals, fitted values, the data used…):

names(model_1)
 [1] "coefficients"  "residuals"     "effects"       "rank"         
 [5] "fitted.values" "assign"        "qr"            "df.residual"  
 [9] "xlevels"       "call"          "terms"         "model"

Reading summary() 🔍

summary() is the classic way to look at a model in the console:

summary(model_1)

Call:

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-6.920 -1.311 -0.018  1.592  6.738 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value            Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  3.26195    0.04664    69.9 <0.0000000000000002 ***
eduyrs       0.14633    0.00331    44.1 <0.0000000000000002 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.34 on 30609 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.0599,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.0598 
F-statistic: 1.95e+03 on 1 and 30609 DF,  p-value: <0.0000000000000002

From top to bottom:

Piece of output What it tells you
Call the model you ran
Residuals distribution of \(y_i - \hat{y}_i\); roughly symmetric around 0 is good
Estimate \(\hat{\beta}\): the estimated intercept and slope
Std. Error the estimated standard deviation of \(\hat{\beta}\) across hypothetical repeated samples (remember last week’s simulation!)
t value Estimate / Std. Error
Pr(>|t|) p-value for \(H_0: \beta = 0\)
Residual standard error typical size of a residual, in units of \(y\)
Multiple R-squared share of the variance in \(y\) “explained” by the model
F-statistic test that all slopes are jointly zero

Activity 💡

\[Immigration\ attitude_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Education_i + \epsilon_i\]

  1. What does the intercept mean? Is it meaningful here?
  2. What does the eduyrs coefficient mean? How much more positive is someone with a university degree (≈ 4 extra years) expected to be?
  3. The \(R^2\) is about 0.06. Does this mean education is “unimportant”?
  4. Does the coefficient carry any causal meaning?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓
  1. The intercept (≈ 3.3) is the predicted attitude for someone with zero years of education. Almost nobody in the data has that, so the intercept is an extrapolation. We fix this below by centering.
  2. Each additional year of education is associated with a ≈ 0.15-point more positive attitude on the 0–10 scale, on average. Four more years: \(4 \times 0.15 \approx 0.6\) points, about a quarter of a standard deviation of the outcome (sd(ess_reg$imwbcnt) ≈ 2.4).
  3. No. \(R^2\) tells us how well we predict individuals, not how strong the association is. Individual attitudes vary for many reasons. Education can still shift the average substantially. Whether you care about \(R^2\) depends on whether your goal is prediction or description/inference.
  4. Not by itself. People with more education differ in many ways (family background, cognitive ability, where they grew up, the jobs they hold). This is a descriptive association. Next week we will use DAGs to say what we would need to assume for a causal reading.

OLS by hand ✍️

There is nothing magical inside lm(). With one predictor, the OLS estimates are:

\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\text{Cov}(x, y)}{\text{Var}(x)} \qquad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]

beta_1 <- cov(ess_reg$eduyrs, ess_reg$imwbcnt) / var(ess_reg$eduyrs)
beta_0 <- mean(ess_reg$imwbcnt) - beta_1 * mean(ess_reg$eduyrs)

c(beta_0 = beta_0, beta_1 = beta_1)
beta_0 beta_1 
3.2619 0.1463 
coef(model_1) # identical
(Intercept)      eduyrs 
     3.2619      0.1463

With multiple predictors, the same idea in matrix form is \(\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y\). Try solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y with X <- model.matrix(model_1) if you want to see it.

Tidy model output with {broom} 🧹

summary() is great for reading in the console, but its output is hard to reuse (for plots, tables, or simulations). The {broom} package turns models into data frames:

  • broom::tidy(): one row per coefficient
  • broom::glance(): one row per model (fit statistics)
  • broom::augment(): one row per observation (fitted values, residuals)
broom::tidy(model_1, conf.int = TRUE)
broom::glance(model_1)
broom::augment(model_1) %>%
  dplyr::select(imwbcnt, eduyrs, .fitted, .resid) %>%
  head()

Making the intercept meaningful: centering 🎯

If we subtract a meaningful value from \(x\), the slope does not change, but the intercept becomes the prediction at that value. Twelve years is roughly the end of secondary school:

model_1c <- lm(imwbcnt ~ I(eduyrs - 12), data = ess_reg)
coef(model_1c)
   (Intercept) I(eduyrs - 12) 
        5.0179         0.1463

I() tells R to compute the expression inside it as is within a formula.

Binary and categorical predictors 🔢

A binary predictor is a difference in means

What happens when \(x\) only takes the values 0 and 1? Let’s regress attitudes on whether the respondent was born abroad:

model_born <- lm(imwbcnt ~ born_abroad, data = ess_reg)
coef(model_born)
(Intercept) born_abroad 
      5.116       1.176

Activity 💡

Compute the mean of imwbcnt for respondents born in the country and born abroad with group_by() and summarize(). How do these means relate to the regression coefficients?

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess_reg %>%
  dplyr::group_by(born_abroad) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_imm = mean(imwbcnt), .groups = "drop")
  • The intercept is the mean for the reference group (born_abroad = 0).
  • The slope is the difference in means between the two groups.

With a binary regressor, OLS is literally a difference in means, and its t-test is (almost exactly) a two-sample t-test. We will come back to this next week, when the binary variable is a treatment.

Categorical predictors and reference categories

When a predictor is a factor, lm() creates one dummy for each level except the first, the reference category:

model_res <- lm(imwbcnt ~ residence, data = ess_reg)
broom::tidy(model_res)

Each coefficient is the difference between that group and big-city residents.

To change the reference category, reorder the factor levels with forcats::fct_relevel():

ess_reg %>%
  dplyr::mutate(residence = forcats::fct_relevel(residence, "Rural")) %>%
  lm(imwbcnt ~ residence, data = .) %>%
  broom::tidy()

(The . passes the piped data frame to the data = argument, because data is not the first argument of lm().)

⚠️ Common mistake: if a categorical variable is stored as numbers (e.g., domicil coded 1–5), lm() treats it as a continuous variable and estimates one slope, assuming that going from “big city” (1) to “suburbs” (2) is the same as going from “village” (4) to “farm” (5). Check the class of your variables, or wrap them in factor().

Multiple regression 🧮

Adding covariates

Education is correlated with many other things that also predict immigration attitudes: age (younger cohorts studied longer), income, where people live, and whether they are immigrants themselves.

\[Attitude_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Educ_i + \beta_2 Age_i + \beta_3 Female_i + \beta_4 BornAbroad_i + \beta_5 Income_i + \beta_{6,7} Residence_i + \epsilon_i\]

model_2 <- lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs + agea + female + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
              data = ess_reg)
summary(model_2)

Call:
lm(formula = imwbcnt ~ eduyrs + agea + female + born_abroad + 
    hinctnta + residence, data = ess_reg)

eduyrs          0.127008   0.003626   35.03 < 0.0000000000000002 ***
agea           -0.003290   0.000763   -4.31   0.0000161615032714 ***
female         -0.002617   0.026517   -0.10                 0.92    
born_abroad     1.081875   0.044113   24.53 < 0.0000000000000002 ***

Activity 💡

  1. Interpret the coefficient on eduyrs. How does it compare to model_1?
  2. Interpret the coefficient on born_abroad.
  3. Interpret the coefficient on residenceRural.
➨ Click for Answer 🔓
  1. Comparing respondents with the same age, gender, migration background, income decile, and type of residence, one more year of education is associated with a ≈ 0.13-point more positive attitude. It is only slightly smaller than in the bivariate model, so the covariates we added explain little of the education gradient.
  2. Respondents born abroad are ≈ 1.1 points more positive than natives with the same education, age, gender, income, and residence.
  3. Rural residents are ≈ 0.26 points more negative than comparable big-city residents.

Note the language: “comparing respondents with the same…”, “is associated with”. We describe conditional associations. We do not (yet) say “causes”.

What does “holding constant” mean? Regression anatomy 🔬

The phrase “holding everything else constant” hides something precise. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (the “regression anatomy” formula) says that the coefficient on education in model_2 equals the slope from a two-step procedure:

  1. Regress education on all other covariates and keep the residuals. This is the part of education that the other covariates cannot predict.
  2. Regress the outcome on those residuals.
# step 1: residualize education
edu_resid <- lm(eduyrs ~ agea + female + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
                data = ess_reg) %>%
  residuals()

# step 2: regress the outcome on the residualized education
coef(lm(ess_reg$imwbcnt ~ edu_resid))["edu_resid"]
edu_resid 
    0.127 
coef(model_2)["eduyrs"] # the same
eduyrs 
 0.127

The multiple regression coefficient only uses the variation in education that is not shared with the controls. This has two consequences:

  • It explains why adding controls can change a coefficient a lot, a little, or not at all.
  • If a control absorbs most of the variation in \(x\) (e.g., occupation “controls away” education), the coefficient is estimated from very little information, and its meaning can change completely. Next week’s DAGs will tell us which variables we should and should not hold constant.

Interactions 🔀

Is the education gradient the same for natives and for people born abroad? A model with an interaction lets the slope of education differ by group:

\[Attitude_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Educ_i + \beta_2 BornAbroad_i + \beta_3 (Educ_i \times BornAbroad_i) + \ldots\]

In R, x * z expands to x + z + x:z (both constituent terms and their product):

model_3 <- lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs * born_abroad + agea + female + hinctnta + residence,
              data = ess_reg)

broom::tidy(model_3) %>%
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(term, "eduyrs|born_abroad"))

Activity 💡

  1. What is the slope of education for natives?
  2. What is the slope of education for respondents born abroad?
  3. Can we interpret the coefficient on born_abroad as “the difference between immigrants and natives”?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓
  1. For natives (born_abroad = 0), the interaction term drops out: the slope is the eduyrs coefficient, ≈ 0.14.
  2. For respondents born abroad: eduyrs + eduyrs:born_abroad ≈ 0.14 − 0.07 ≈ 0.07. The education gradient is about half as steep.
  3. No. In an interaction model, the born_abroad coefficient is the difference between immigrants and natives when education = 0, which is an extrapolation. This is the core point of Brambor, Clark & Golder (2006): constituent terms are conditional effects. Compute the quantity you care about explicitly, which is what {marginaleffects} is for.

Slopes, predictions, and plots with {marginaleffects} 📐

Doing arithmetic on coefficients by hand gets error-prone quickly, and it is even worse for the non-linear models in Week 6. The {marginaleffects} package computes the quantities we care about directly, with standard errors.

The slope of education in each group:

marginaleffects::avg_slopes(model_3, variables = "eduyrs", by = "born_abroad")

 born_abroad Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)     S  2.5 % 97.5 %
           0   0.1359    0.00386 35.21   <0.001 899.5 0.1283 0.1434
           1   0.0699    0.00930  7.51   <0.001  44.0 0.0516 0.0881

Term: eduyrs
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

Predicted values for hypothetical respondents. datagrid() sets the variables we specify and holds the rest at their means (numeric) or modes (categorical):

marginaleffects::predictions(
  model_3,
  newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(eduyrs = c(9, 12, 16, 20), born_abroad = c(0, 1))
)

 eduyrs born_abroad Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
      9           0     4.37     0.0295 148.1   <0.001 Inf  4.31   4.43
      9           1     5.77     0.0661  87.4   <0.001 Inf  5.64   5.90
     12           0     4.78     0.0253 189.2   <0.001 Inf  4.73   4.83
     12           1     5.98     0.0510 117.3   <0.001 Inf  5.88   6.08
     16           0     5.32     0.0273 195.0   <0.001 Inf  5.27   5.38
     16           1     6.26     0.0517 121.1   <0.001 Inf  6.16   6.36
     20           0     5.87     0.0365 160.9   <0.001 Inf  5.79   5.94
     20           1     6.54     0.0743  88.1   <0.001 Inf  6.40   6.69

Type: response

A plot of the predictions:

marginaleffects::plot_predictions(model_3,
                                  condition = list("eduyrs", "born_abroad" = c(0, 1))) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Years of education",
       y = "Predicted attitude (0-10)",
       color = "Born abroad", fill = "Born abroad")

The base R equivalent of predictions() is predict(model, newdata = data.frame(...)). It works, but you have to supply every variable in the model yourself, and you do not get standard errors for most models.

Activity 💡

Using model_2, what is the expected difference in attitudes between a 25-year-old and a 65-year-old with 16 years of education, holding everything else at typical values?

Hint: marginaleffects::predictions() with datagrid(agea = c(25, 65), eduyrs = 16), or marginaleffects::comparisons() with variables = list(agea = c(25, 65)).

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
marginaleffects::predictions(model_2,
                             newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(agea = c(25, 65),
                                                                 eduyrs = 16))

 agea eduyrs Estimate Std. Error   z Pr(>|z|)   S 2.5 % 97.5 %
   25     16     5.39     0.0333 161   <0.001 Inf  5.32   5.45
   65     16     5.25     0.0292 180   <0.001 Inf  5.20   5.31

Type: response
marginaleffects::comparisons(model_2,
                             variables = list(agea = c(25, 65)),
                             newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(eduyrs = 16))

 eduyrs Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S  2.5 %  97.5 %
     16   -0.132     0.0305 -4.31   <0.001 15.9 -0.191 -0.0718

Term: agea
Type: response
Comparison: 65 - 25

The 65-year-old is expected to be ≈ 0.13 points less positive, a small difference. Because model_2 is linear and has no age interactions, the difference is simply \(40 \times \hat{\beta}_{age}\), whatever the education level.

Uncertainty 🎲

Which standard errors?

The standard errors from summary() assume homoskedastic and independent errors. Survey data usually violate both:

  • Heteroskedasticity: the spread of attitudes may differ across education levels.
  • Clustering: respondents in the same country share context, so their errors are correlated.

We can ask for different variance estimators without re-estimating the model. {modelsummary} accepts a vcov argument, and so does {marginaleffects}:

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  list("Classical" = model_2, "Robust (HC2)" = model_2, "Clustered by country" = model_2),
  vcov = list("classical", "HC2", ~cntry),
  coef_omit = "Intercept",
  gof_map = c("nobs", "vcov.type")
)
Classical Robust (HC2) Clustered by country
eduyrs 0.127 0.127 0.127
(0.004) (0.004) (0.013)
agea -0.003 -0.003 -0.003
(0.001) (0.001) (0.002)
female -0.003 -0.003 -0.003
(0.027) (0.027) (0.043)
born_abroad 1.082 1.082 1.082
(0.044) (0.045) (0.161)
hinctnta 0.031 0.031 0.031
(0.005) (0.005) (0.011)
residenceTown 0.021 0.021 0.021
(0.034) (0.034) (0.102)
residenceRural -0.258 -0.258 -0.258
(0.032) (0.033) (0.115)
Num.Obs. 30611 30611 30611
Std.Errors IID HC2 by: cntry

The point estimates are identical, and only the standard errors change. The clustered ones are almost four times larger. With 24 countries, even clustered standard errors are somewhat unreliable (few clusters), which is one of the motivations for the multilevel models in Week 7.

King & Roberts (2015), on this week’s optional list: when robust and classical standard errors differ a lot, that is a symptom that something in the model may be misspecified, not only a nuisance to be fixed.

The bootstrap 🥾

The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution by simulation: we treat our sample as if it were the population, draw many samples with replacement from it, re-estimate the model each time, and look at how much the coefficient varies. This is last week’s simulation with our own data standing in for the population.

bootstrap_educ <- function(data) {
  boot_df <- dplyr::slice_sample(data, prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  boot_model <- lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs + agea + female + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
                   data = boot_df)
  coef(boot_model)["eduyrs"]
}

boot_coefs <- purrr::map_dbl(1:500, \(i) bootstrap_educ(ess_reg))

sd(boot_coefs) # bootstrap standard error
[1] 0.003791
quantile(boot_coefs, c(0.025, 0.975)) # percentile 95% confidence interval
  2.5%  97.5% 
0.1199 0.1342

Compare it with the analytical robust standard error:

broom::tidy(model_2) %>% dplyr::filter(term == "eduyrs") # classical
sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(model_2, type = "HC2")))["eduyrs"] # robust
  eduyrs 
0.003639 
ggplot(data.frame(boot_coefs), aes(x = boot_coefs)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2f1a61", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = coef(model_2)["eduyrs"], color = "#cc0065", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Bootstrapped coefficient on education",
       y = "Count",
       title = "500 bootstrap replications of model 2")

Bonus activity 💡

Our bootstrap resamples individuals, so it matches the robust standard errors, not the clustered ones. How would you write a cluster bootstrap that resamples whole countries?

Hint: sample 24 country codes with replacement, then collect the respondents of each sampled country with purrr::map() + dplyr::bind_rows().

➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
bootstrap_educ_cluster <- function(data) {
  countries <- unique(data$cntry)
  sampled <- sample(countries, size = length(countries), replace = TRUE)
  boot_df <- purrr::map(sampled, \(c) dplyr::filter(data, cntry == c)) %>%
    dplyr::bind_rows()
  coef(lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs + agea + female + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
          data = boot_df))["eduyrs"]
}

boot_cluster <- purrr::map_dbl(1:200, \(i) bootstrap_educ_cluster(ess_reg))
sd(boot_cluster)
[1] 0.01303

The cluster-bootstrap standard error is several times the individual one and close to the analytical clustered standard error in the previous table. Once we acknowledge that respondents come in country clusters, 30,000 respondents carry far less information than 30,000 independent draws would. With 24 clusters, bootstrap-based inference is also imperfect, but the exercise shows what the clustered standard error is trying to capture.

Regression tables with {modelsummary} 📋

Every paper you write will have regression tables. Never copy numbers by hand: generate tables from code, so that when the data or model changes (and it will), the table updates too.

modelsummary::modelsummary() takes a (named) list of models:

models <- list(
  "Bivariate" = model_1,
  "Controls" = model_2,
  "Interaction" = model_3
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  models,
  vcov = ~cntry, # cluster by country
  coef_map = c(
    "eduyrs" = "Years of education",
    "born_abroad" = "Born abroad",
    "eduyrs:born_abroad" = "Education × Born abroad",
    "agea" = "Age",
    "female" = "Female",
    "hinctnta" = "Household income (decile)",
    "residenceTown" = "Town (ref. big city)",
    "residenceRural" = "Rural (ref. big city)",
    "(Intercept)" = "Constant"
  ),
  stars = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  title = "Education and attitudes toward immigration (ESS Round 11)",
  notes = "OLS. Outcome: immigrants make country a worse (0) or better (10) place to live. Standard errors clustered by country in parentheses."
)

A few things to notice:

  • coef_map renames and orders the coefficients, and drops any not listed.
  • vcov is applied to all models.
  • add_rows (not used here) adds rows that are not coefficients, e.g., “Controls: Yes/No”.
  • Stars are a convention, not a requirement. Many journals now prefer to show only standard errors or confidence intervals: statistic = "conf.int".

Exporting: the same call with output = writes the table to a file ready for your paper:

modelsummary::modelsummary(models, output = "output/tables/table_1.docx") # Word
modelsummary::modelsummary(models, output = "output/tables/table_1.tex")  # LaTeX

Descriptive statistics tables

{modelsummary} also produces the “Table 1” of descriptive statistics that almost every paper includes:

ess_reg %>%
  dplyr::select(imwbcnt, eduyrs, agea, female, born_abroad, hinctnta) %>%
  modelsummary::datasummary_skim(type = "numeric")

Bonus: survey weights ⚖️

lm() accepts a weights argument, so you can run lm(imwbcnt ~ eduyrs, data = ess_reg, weights = anweight). Whether regressions should be weighted is less obvious than for descriptive statistics. It depends on whether you are after a population-average quantity and on whether effects are heterogeneous. Solon, Haider & Wooldridge (2015), “What Are We Weighting For?”, is an accessible guide. For design-based standard errors, look at the {survey} and {srvyr} packages.

Your turn 🚀

Activity 💡

Using ess (remember to define a common analysis sample!):

  1. Pick a different outcome: satisfaction with democracy (stfdem) or trust in politicians (trstplt).
  2. Estimate three models: bivariate with education, adding socio-demographic controls, and adding an interaction between education and gender (female).
  3. Produce a publication-ready table with modelsummary(), with clustered standard errors and readable coefficient names.
  4. Write two sentences interpreting the education coefficient in the final model. Is your interpretation descriptive, predictive, or causal? What would you need to assume to make it causal?
➨ Click for Answer 🔓 
ess_dem <- ess %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(stfdem, eduyrs, agea, female, born_abroad, hinctnta, residence)

dem_models <- list(
  "Bivariate" = lm(stfdem ~ eduyrs, data = ess_dem),
  "Controls" = lm(stfdem ~ eduyrs + agea + female + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
                  data = ess_dem),
  "Interaction" = lm(stfdem ~ eduyrs * female + agea + born_abroad + hinctnta + residence,
                     data = ess_dem)
)

modelsummary::modelsummary(
  dem_models,
  vcov = ~cntry,
  coef_map = c("eduyrs" = "Years of education", "female" = "Female",
               "eduyrs:female" = "Education × Female", "agea" = "Age",
               "born_abroad" = "Born abroad", "hinctnta" = "Household income (decile)"),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"),
  notes = "OLS. Outcome: satisfaction with democracy (0-10). SEs clustered by country."
)
